planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring or fall into amended, well-drained soil, setting the bud union at or just below grade in cold climates.

directions: Set plants where they receive at least six hours of direct sun and good air circulation to limit blackspot, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. This David Austin English rose produces large, intensely fragrant, old-fashioned rosette blooms in deep pink over repeated flushes from late spring through fall. Prune hard in late winter to encourage strong new flowering canes, and feed monthly through the growing season for the best repeat bloom. It can be grown as a bushy shrub or trained as a short climber against a wall or fence.

planting.note: Plant in early spring or fall in full sun and well-drained soil; this tough shrub tolerates poorer soil and less fussing than hybrid teas.

directions: Bonica was the first shrub rose to win the All-America Rose Selections award and remains a benchmark for easy-care landscape roses. It bears clusters of soft pink, lightly fragrant double blooms almost continuously from late spring to frost, followed by ornamental orange hips if deadheading is skipped late in the season. Give it full sun and average garden soil; established plants need only light pruning in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood. Its disease resistance and dense, rounded habit make it a reliable choice for hedges, borders, or mass plantings.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or potted roses in spring or fall in a sunny, well-drained bed; this tall, vigorous grower benefits from extra spacing and a sturdy support-free habit.

directions: Introduced in 1954 and named for the newly crowned British monarch, this cultivar founded the Grandiflora class by combining hybrid tea flower form with floribunda-style clustered blooms. It produces high-centered, clear pink flowers on tall, upright canes that make it excellent for the back of a border or as an informal hedge. Give it full sun, regular feeding, and deep watering, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage the next flush. Its height and vigor mean it benefits from more room than typical hybrid teas and only moderate winter pruning.

planting.note: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, angling canes at planting to encourage horizontal training and better bloom coverage.

directions: An AARS winner from 1957, this climber is prized for its comparatively thornless canes and its ability to bloom well even in partial shade or against a north-facing wall. Semi-double, ruffled golden-yellow flowers open from pointed buds and repeat reliably through the season with light fragrance. Train and tie the flexible canes horizontally along a support to maximize flowering laterals, and prune lightly after the main structure is established. It is a popular choice for arbors, pillars, and fences where a moderately sized, well-behaved climber is needed.

planting.note: Plant with the crown two to three inches below soil level to help the vine recover from stem dieback, keeping roots shaded and cool while the top grows into sun.

directions: Introduced in France in 1899, this heirloom clematis bears bright carmine-red blooms with a paler central bar, fading slightly as they age through summer. As a pruning group three cultivar, cut all stems back hard to a strong pair of buds about a foot from the ground in late winter, which keeps the vine compact and floriferous. Provide a trellis, obelisk, or shrub to climb, and keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist. It flowers on new growth from midsummer into fall, making it a reliable companion for climbing roses that bloom earlier in the season.

planting.note: Plant deeply with the crown below soil level and shade the roots with mulch or low companion plants, allowing the vine to climb into full sun above.

directions: Dating to 1876, this antique clematis produces fully double, pure white rosette-shaped flowers with a light green tint that carry a fresh, sweet fragrance rare among large-flowered clematis. It flowers earliest in the season on old wood, so prune lightly right after the first flush to shape the vine and encourage a smaller repeat bloom on new growth later in summer. Give it fertile, well-drained soil and a sturdy support such as a trellis or pergola post. Because its doubled flowers can be sparse in cooler climates, siting it in a warm, sheltered spot improves flower quality.

planting.note: Set the crown two to three inches deep at planting time to protect against clematis wilt, and mulch the root zone while letting the top growth reach for sun.

directions: This French-bred cultivar is valued for its velvety, deep ruby-red blooms with contrasting cream-yellow anthers, produced in flushes from early to late summer. As a pruning group three vine, cut all stems back to a strong bud pair roughly twelve inches above the soil in late winter each year to keep growth vigorous and floriferous. It performs best with its roots shaded and cool and its foliage and flowers reaching into full sun on a trellis, fence, or through a shrub. Regular moisture and an annual topdressing of compost help sustain its rich color through the season.

planting.note: Plant deeply with the crown a couple of inches below grade and provide immediate support, since this is a vigorous grower that quickly climbs once established.

directions: A French introduction from the early twentieth century, this reliable clematis produces abundant mauve-pink flowers with a subtle darker central bar and golden stamens over a long summer bloom period. It belongs to pruning group three, so cut stems back hard to a healthy bud pair near the base in late winter to keep the vigorous vine tidy and encourage maximum flowering. It tolerates a range of soils better than many large-flowered hybrids as long as drainage is adequate, and it is often recommended as an easy, forgiving choice for beginners. Pair it with a host shrub or sturdy trellis, since its long stems can reach considerable height in a single season.
